e-213.knowledge_point: Finding a Moment in Time When a Particle is Stationary
e-213.problem:
The position $s(t)$ of a particle (in meters) at time $t$ seconds is given by 

$$
s(t) = -\frac{1}{3}t^3 + \frac{5}{2}t^2 + 6t + 1,\quad t\geq 0.
$$

Calculate the time at which the particle is stationary, and give the displacement of the particle from the origin at this time.
e-213.worked_solution:
The particle is stationary when its velocity is zero. So first, we need to calculate the velocity function. We can do that by taking the derivative of the position function, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\frac{1}{3}{t}^{3}+\frac{5}{2}{t}^{2}+6t+1) \\  & =-{t}^{2}+5t+6\end{aligned}
$$

The particle is stationary when $v=0\, \textrm{m/s}$. So, we set $v = 0$ and solve for $t \mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =-{t}^{2}+5t+6 \\ 0 & ={t}^{2}-5t-6 \\ 0 & =(t-6)(t+1)\end{aligned}
$$

The solutions are $t=6$ and $t=-1.$ Since $t\geq 0,$ we discard the solution $t=-1$ and keep only $t=6.$

So the particle is stationary only at $t=6\, \textrm{s}.$ To find the displacement from the origin at this time, we substitute $t=6$ back into $s(t)$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}s(6) & =-\frac{1}{3}\cdot {6}^{3}+\frac{5}{2}\cdot {6}^{2}+6\cdot 6+1 \\  & =-72+90+36+1 \\  & =55\,\text{m}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particle is stationary at $t = 6\, \textrm{s}$ and its displacement from the origin at this time is $55\, \textrm{m}.$

e-6159.knowledge_point: Determining Intervals of Increasing or Decreasing Displacement
e-6159.problem: The displacement $s,$ in meters, relative to a fixed origin $O$ of a particle moving in a straight line along the $x$-axis is given by $s(t) = t^4 - 32t$, where $t \geq 0$ is the time measured in seconds. Determine the time intervals in which the particle is moving in the direction of decreasing $x.$
e-6159.worked_solution:
If the particle moves in the direction of decreasing $x,$ then its velocity is negative. 

First, we calculate the velocity function by differentiating the position function:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{4}-32t) \\  & =4{t}^{3}-32\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate time intervals in which the particle is moving in the direction of decreasing $x$, we solve the inequality $v(t) <    0\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & <0 \\ 4{t}^{3}-32 & <0 \\ 4{t}^{3} & <32 \\ {t}^{3} & <8 \\ t & <2\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the time interval in which the particle is moving to the direction of decreasing $x$ is $t\in\left[ 0, 2\right).$

e-217.knowledge_point: Calculating the Velocity of a Particle at the Moment When Its Acceleration is Zero
e-217.problem:
A particle $P$ is traveling along the $x$-axis with displacement $s(t)$ from a fixed origin $O$ given by

$$
s(t) = t^3-3t^2+12t,\quad t\geq 0.
$$

Find the time at which the acceleration is zero, and find the value of the velocity at this moment.
e-217.worked_solution:
First, we calculate $v(t)$ by differentiating $s(t)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-3{t}^{2}+12t) \\  & =3{t}^{2}-6t+12\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we differentiate $v(t)$ to find $a(t)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2}-6t+12) \\  & =6t-6\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we put $a=0$ to find the time when the acceleration is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =6t-6 \\ 6t & =6 \\ t & =1\end{aligned}
$$

So the acceleration is zero when $t=1$. To find the velocity at this moment, we substitute this back into $v(t)$ to get

$$
v(1) = 3(1)^2 - 6(1)+12 = 9.
$$

after.name: Question 1
after.problem:
The position $s(t)$ of a particle (in meters) at time $t$ seconds is given by 

$$
s(t)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({t}^{2}-6t+10),\,t\ge 0.

before.html:
Question 2
?

The position s(t) of a particle (in meters) at time t seconds is given by s(t)=(t−3)et,t≥0. Calculate the time at which the particle is stationary.

a
t=2s
b
t=3e2s
c
t=32s
d
t=3s
e
t=2e2s
Submit

decision.explanation: The particle is stationary when s'(t)=0. By the product rule, s'(t)=e^t+(t-3)e^t=(t-2)e^t. Since e^t is always positive, t-2=0, giving t=2 s.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem:
The position $s(t)$ of a particle (in meters) at time $t$ seconds is given by 

$$
s(t)=(t-3){e}^{t},\,t\ge 0.
$$

Calculate the time at which the particle is stationary.
after.worked_solution:
The particle is stationary when its velocity is zero. So first, we need to calculate the velocity function. We can do that by taking the derivative of the position function, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}((t-3){e}^{t}) \\  & ={e}^{t}+(t-3){e}^{t} \\  & =(t-2){e}^{t}\end{aligned}
$$

The particle is stationary when $v=0\,\text{m/s}.$ So, we set $v=0$ and solve for $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(t-2){e}^{t} & =0 \\ t-2 & =0 \\ t & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particle is stationary at $t=2\,\text{s}.$

after.name: Question 4
after.problem:
The position $s(t)$ of a particle at time $t$ is given by 

$$
s(t)={t}^{2}-2t+8,\,t\ge 0.
$$

Calculate the time when the particle is stationary, and give the displacement of the particle from the origin at this time.
after.worked_solution:
The particle is stationary when its velocity is zero. So first, we need to calculate the velocity function. We can do that by taking the derivative of the position function, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-2t+8) \\  & =2t-2\end{aligned}
$$

The particle is stationary when $v=0$ So, we set $v=0$ and solve for $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2t-2 & =0 \\ 2t & =2 \\ t & =1\end{aligned}
$$

So the particle is stationary only at $t=1.$ To find the displacement from the origin at this time, we substitute $t=1$ back into $s(t)$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}s(1) & ={1}^{2}-2(1)+8 \\  & =1-2+8 \\  & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particle is stationary at $t=1$ and its displacement from the origin at this time is $7.$

after.html:
Question 4
?

The position s(t) of a particle at time t is given by s(t)=t2−2t+8,t≥0. Calculate the time when the particle is stationary, and give the displacement of the particle from the origin at this time.

a
t=2,s=8
b
t=3,s=11
c
t=1,s=10
d
t=1,s=7
e
t=3,s=9
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The particle is stationary when its velocity is zero. So first, we need to calculate the velocity function. We can do that by taking the derivative of the position function, as follows:

v(t)=dsdt=ddt(t2−2t+8)=2t−2

The particle is stationary when v=0 So, we set v=0 and solve for t: 2t−2=02t=2t=1

So the particle is stationary only at t=1. To find the displacement from the origin at this time, we substitute t=1 back into s(t) and get s(1)=12−2(1)+8=1−2+8=7.

Therefore, the particle is stationary at t=1 and its displacement from the origin at this time is 7.

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Moment in Time When a Particle is Stationary
content.problem:
The position $s(t)$ of a particle at time $t$ is given by 

$$
s(t)={t}^{2}-2t+8,\,t\ge 0.
$$

Calculate the time when the particle is stationary, and give the displacement of the particle from the origin at this time.
content.worked_solution:
The particle is stationary when its velocity is zero. So first, we need to calculate the velocity function. We can do that by taking the derivative of the position function, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-2t+8) \\  & =2t-2\end{aligned}
$$

The particle is stationary when $v=0$ So, we set $v=0$ and solve for $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2t-2 & =0 \\ 2t & =2 \\ t & =1\end{aligned}
$$

So the particle is stationary only at $t=1.$ To find the displacement from the origin at this time, we substitute $t=1$ back into $s(t)$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}s(1) & ={1}^{2}-2(1)+8 \\  & =1-2+8 \\  & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particle is stationary at $t=1$ and its displacement from the origin at this time is $7.$

before.html:
Question 5
?

The position s(t) of a particle (in meters) at time t seconds is given by s(t)=t2ln⁡t,t>0. Calculate the time at which the particle is stationary.

a
t=1es
b
t=es
c
t=es
d
t=1s
e
t=12es
Submit

decision.explanation: Using the product rule, v(t)=s'(t)=2t ln(t)+t=t(2 ln(t)+1). Since t>0, velocity is zero when ln(t)=-1/2, giving t=e^(-1/2)=1/√e seconds.

after.name: Question 5
after.problem:
The position $s(t)$ of a particle (in meters) at time $t$ seconds is given by 

$$
s(t)={t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t,\,t>0.
$$

Calculate the time at which the particle is stationary.
after.worked_solution:
The particle is stationary when its velocity is zero. So first, we need to calculate the velocity function. We can do that by taking the derivative of the position function, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t) \\  & =2t\operatorname{ln}⁡t+{t}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{t} \\  & =2t\operatorname{ln}⁡t+t \\  & =t(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t+1)\end{aligned}
$$

The particle is stationary when $v=0\,\text{m/s}.$ So, we set $v=0$ and solve for $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t+1) & =0 \\ 2\operatorname{ln}⁡t+1 & =0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡t & =-\frac{1}{2} \\ t & ={e}^{-1/2} \\ t & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{e}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particle is stationary at $t=\frac{1}{\sqrt{e}}\,\text{s}.$

Question 5
?

The position s(t) of a particle (in meters) at time t seconds is given by s(t)=t2ln⁡t,t>0. Calculate the time at which the particle is stationary.

a
t=1es
b
t=es
c
t=es
d
t=1s
e
t=12es
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The particle is stationary when its velocity is zero. So first, we need to calculate the velocity function. We can do that by taking the derivative of the position function, as follows: v(t)=dsdt=ddt(t2ln⁡t)=2tln⁡t+t2⋅1t=2tln⁡t+t=t(2ln⁡t+1)

The particle is stationary when v=0m/s. So, we set v=0 and solve for t: t(2ln⁡t+1)=02ln⁡t+1=0ln⁡t=−12t=e−1/2t=1e

Therefore, the particle is stationary at t=1es.

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Moment in Time When a Particle is Stationary
content.problem:
The position $s(t)$ of a particle (in meters) at time $t$ seconds is given by 

$$
s(t)={t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t,\,t>0.
$$

Calculate the time at which the particle is stationary.
content.worked_solution:
The particle is stationary when its velocity is zero. So first, we need to calculate the velocity function. We can do that by taking the derivative of the position function, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t) \\  & =2t\operatorname{ln}⁡t+{t}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{t} \\  & =2t\operatorname{ln}⁡t+t \\  & =t(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t+1)\end{aligned}
$$

The particle is stationary when $v=0\,\text{m/s}.$ So, we set $v=0$ and solve for $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t+1) & =0 \\ 2\operatorname{ln}⁡t+1 & =0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡t & =-\frac{1}{2} \\ t & ={e}^{-1/2} \\ t & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{e}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particle is stationary at $t=\frac{1}{\sqrt{e}}\,\text{s}.$

Question 6
?

The displacement s (in meters) relative to a fixed origin O of a particle moving in a straight line along the x-axis is given by s(t)=(4t−7)et, where t≥0 is the time measured in seconds. Determine the time intervals in which the particle is moving in the direction of increasing x.

a
 (4,∞)
b
[0,56)
c
(2,134)
d
[0,53) and (72,∞)
e
(34,∞)
Submit

decision.explanation: Increasing x requires positive velocity. By the product rule, v(t)=4e^t+(4t-7)e^t=(4t-3)e^t. Since e^t>0, v(t)>0 exactly when t>3/4.

after.name: Question 6
after.problem: The displacement $s$ (in meters) relative to a fixed origin $O$ of a particle moving in a straight line along the $x$-axis is given by $s(t)=(4t-7){e}^{t}$, where $t\ge 0$ is the time measured in seconds. Determine the time intervals in which the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x.$
after.worked_solution:
If the particle moves in the direction of increasing $x,$ then its velocity is positive.

First, we calculate the velocity function by differentiating the position function:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}((4t-7){e}^{t}) \\  & =(4t-3){e}^{t}\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate time intervals in which the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x$, we solve $v(t)>0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & >0 \\ (4t-3){e}^{t} & >0 \\ 4t-3 & >0 \\ t & >\frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the time interval in which the particle is moving to the direction of increasing $x$ is $(\frac{3}{4},\infty ).$

Question 6

The displacement s (in meters) relative to a fixed origin O of a particle moving in a straight line along the x-axis is given by s(t)=(4t−7)et, where t≥0 is the time measured in seconds. Determine the time intervals in which the particle is moving in the direction of increasing x.

a
 (4,∞)
b
[0,56)
c
(2,134)
d
[0,53) and (72,∞)
e
(34,∞)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

If the particle moves in the direction of increasing x, then its velocity is positive.

First, we calculate the velocity function by differentiating the position function: v(t)=dsdt=ddt((4t−7)et)=(4t−3)et

To calculate time intervals in which the particle is moving in the direction of increasing x, we solve v(t)>0: v(t)>0(4t−3)et>04t−3>0t>34

Hence, the time interval in which the particle is moving to the direction of increasing x is (34,∞).

content.knowledge_point: Determining Intervals of Increasing or Decreasing Displacement
content.problem: The displacement $s$ (in meters) relative to a fixed origin $O$ of a particle moving in a straight line along the $x$-axis is given by $s(t)=(4t-7){e}^{t}$, where $t\ge 0$ is the time measured in seconds. Determine the time intervals in which the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x.$
content.worked_solution:
If the particle moves in the direction of increasing $x,$ then its velocity is positive.

First, we calculate the velocity function by differentiating the position function:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}((4t-7){e}^{t}) \\  & =(4t-3){e}^{t}\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate time intervals in which the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x$, we solve $v(t)>0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & >0 \\ (4t-3){e}^{t} & >0 \\ 4t-3 & >0 \\ t & >\frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the time interval in which the particle is moving to the direction of increasing $x$ is $(\frac{3}{4},\infty ).$

Question 7
?

The displacement s (in meters) relative to a fixed origin O of a particle moving in a straight line along the x-axis is given by s(t)=et2−4t+6, where t≥0 is the time measured in seconds. Find the time intervals in which the particle is moving in the direction of decreasing x.

a
[0,1) and (2,+∞)
b
[0,2)
c
(2,+∞)
d
(3,4)
e
(1,2) and (4,8)
Submit

decision.explanation: Decreasing x requires negative velocity. Differentiating gives v(t)=(2t-4)e^{t^2-4t+6}. The exponential is always positive, so v(t)<0 when t<2. With t≥0, the interval is [0,2).

after.name: Question 7
after.problem: The displacement $s$ (in meters) relative to a fixed origin $O$ of a particle moving in a straight line along the $x$-axis is given by $s(t)={e}^{{t}^{2}-4t+6}$, where $t\ge 0$ is the time measured in seconds. Find the time intervals in which the particle is moving in the direction of decreasing $x.$
after.worked_solution:
If the particle moves in the direction of decreasing $x,$ then its velocity is negative.

First, we calculate the velocity function by differentiating the position function:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{{t}^{2}-4t+6}) \\  & =(2t-4){e}^{{t}^{2}-4t+6}\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate time intervals in which the particle is moving in the direction of decreasing $x$, we must solve $v(t)<0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & <0 \\ (2t-4){e}^{{t}^{2}-4t+6} & <0 \\ 2t-4 & <0 \\ 2t & <4 \\ t & <2\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the time interval in which the particle is moving to the direction of decreasing $x$ is $[0,2).$

content.knowledge_point: Determining Intervals of Increasing or Decreasing Displacement
content.problem: The displacement $s$ (in meters) relative to a fixed origin $O$ of a particle moving in a straight line along the $x$-axis is given by $s(t)={e}^{{t}^{2}-4t+6}$, where $t\ge 0$ is the time measured in seconds. Find the time intervals in which the particle is moving in the direction of decreasing $x.$
content.worked_solution:
If the particle moves in the direction of decreasing $x,$ then its velocity is negative.

First, we calculate the velocity function by differentiating the position function:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{{t}^{2}-4t+6}) \\  & =(2t-4){e}^{{t}^{2}-4t+6}\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate time intervals in which the particle is moving in the direction of decreasing $x$, we must solve $v(t)<0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & <0 \\ (2t-4){e}^{{t}^{2}-4t+6} & <0 \\ 2t-4 & <0 \\ 2t & <4 \\ t & <2\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the time interval in which the particle is moving to the direction of decreasing $x$ is $[0,2).$

before.html:
Question 9
?

The displacement s, in meters, relative to a fixed origin O of a particle moving in a straight line along the x-axis is given by s(t)=te−2t, where t≥0 is the time, measured in seconds. Find the time intervals in which the particle is moving in the direction of increasing x.

a
[0,14)
b
[0,1)
c
(12,∞)
d
(14,∞)
e
[0,12)
Submit

decision.explanation: Increasing x requires positive velocity. By the product rule, v(t)=e^{-2t}(1-2t). Since e^{-2t}>0, velocity is positive when t<1/2. With t≥0, the interval is [0,1/2).

after.name: Question 9
after.problem: The displacement $s,$ in meters, relative to a fixed origin $O$ of a particle moving in a straight line along the $x$-axis is given by $s(t)=t{e}^{-2t}$, where $t\ge 0$ is the time, measured in seconds. Find the time intervals in which the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x.$
after.worked_solution:
If the particle moves in the direction of increasing $x,$ then its velocity is positive. 

First, we calculate the velocity function by differentiating the position function:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t{e}^{-2t}) \\  & ={e}^{-2t}(1-2t)\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate time intervals in which the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x$, we solve $v(t)>0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & >0 \\ {e}^{-2t}(1-2t) & >0 \\ 1-2t & >0 \\ 2t & <1 \\ t & <\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the time interval in which the particle is moving to the direction of increasing $x$ is $t\in [0,\frac{1}{2}).$

after.name: Question 11
after.problem:
A particle $P$ is traveling along the $x$-axis with displacement $s(t)$ from a fixed origin $O$ given by

$$
s(t)=\frac{{t}^{3}}{2}-6{t}^{2}+30t+4,\,t\ge 0.
$$

Find the time at which the acceleration is zero, and find the value of the velocity at this moment.
after.worked_solution:
First, we calculate $v(t)$ by differentiating $s(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{t}^{3}}{2}-6{t}^{2}+30t+4) \\  & =\frac{3{t}^{2}}{2}-12t+30\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we differentiate $v(t)$ to find $a(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{3{t}^{2}}{2}-12t+30) \\  & =3t-12\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we put $a=0$ to find the time when the acceleration is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}3t-12 & =0 \\ 3t & =12 \\ t & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the acceleration is zero when $t=4.$ To find the velocity at this moment, we substitute this back into $v(t)$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(4) & =\frac{3(4)^{2}}{2}-12(4)+30 \\  & =24-48+30 \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the acceleration is zero when t=4. To find the velocity at this moment, we substitute this back into v(t) to get v(4)=3(4)22−12(4)+30=24−48+30=6

after.name: Question 12
after.problem:
A particle $P$ is traveling along the $x$-axis with displacement $s(t)$ from a fixed origin $O$ given by

$$
s(t)=-\frac{2}{9}{t}^{3}+3{t}^{2}+14t+17,\,t\ge 0.
$$

Find the time at which the acceleration is zero, and find the value of the velocity at this moment.
after.worked_solution:
First, we calculate $v(t)$ by differentiating $s(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\frac{2}{9}{t}^{3}+3{t}^{2}+14t+17) \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}{t}^{2}+6t+14\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we differentiate $v(t)$ to find $a(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\frac{2}{3}{t}^{2}+6t+14) \\  & =-\frac{4}{3}t+6\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we put $a=0$ to find the time when the acceleration is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =-\frac{4}{3}t+6 \\ \frac{4}{3}t & =6 \\ t & =4.5\end{aligned}
$$

So the acceleration is zero when $t=4.5.$ To find the velocity at this moment, we substitute this back into $v(t)$ to get

$$
v(4.5)=-\frac{2}{3}(4.5)^{2}+6(4.5)+14=27.5.
$$

Question 13
?

A particle P is traveling along the x-axis with displacement s(t) from a fixed origin O given by s(t)=t2ln⁡(t),t≥0. Find the time at which the acceleration is zero, and find the value of the velocity at this moment.

a
t=e−1/2,v=−2e−1/2
b
t=e−3/2,v=−2e−3/2
c
t=e−5/2,v=−2e−5/2
d
t=e−3/2,v=−e−3/2
e
t=e−5/2,v=−e−3/2
Submit

decision.explanation: For t>0, v(t)=2t ln(t)+t and a(t)=2 ln(t)+3. Setting acceleration to zero gives ln(t)=-3/2, hence t=e^{-3/2}. At this time, v=t(2 ln(t)+1)=-2e^{-3/2}.

after.name: Question 13
after.problem:
A particle $P$ is traveling along the $x$-axis with displacement $s(t)$ from a fixed origin $O$ given by

$$
s(t)={t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(t),\,t\ge 0.
$$

Find the time at which the acceleration is zero, and find the value of the velocity at this moment.
after.worked_solution:
First, we calculate $v(t)$ by differentiating $s(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(t)) \\  & =2t\operatorname{ln}⁡(t)+t\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we differentiate $v(t)$ to find $a(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+2t\operatorname{ln}⁡(t)) \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡(t)+3\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we put $a=0$ to find the time when the acceleration is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡(t)+3 \\ 2\operatorname{ln}⁡(t) & =-3 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(t) & =-\frac{3}{2} \\ t & ={e}^{-3/2}\end{aligned}
$$

So the acceleration is zero when $t={e}^{-3/2}.$ To find the velocity at this moment, we substitute this back into $v(t)$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}v({e}^{-3/2}) & =2({e}^{-3/2})\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-3/2})+{e}^{-3/2} \\  & =2{e}^{-3/2}(-\frac{3}{2})+{e}^{-3/2} \\  & =-2{e}^{-3/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 13
?

A particle P is traveling along the x-axis with displacement s(t) from a fixed origin O given by s(t)=t2ln⁡(t),t≥0. Find the time at which the acceleration is zero, and find the value of the velocity at this moment.

a
t=e−1/2,v=−2e−1/2
b
t=e−3/2,v=−2e−3/2
c
t=e−5/2,v=−2e−5/2
d
t=e−3/2,v=−e−3/2
e
t=e−5/2,v=−e−3/2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we calculate v(t) by differentiating s(t):

v(t)=dsdt=ddt(t2ln⁡(t))=2tln⁡(t)+t

Now, we differentiate v(t) to find a(t): a(t)=dvdt=ddt(t+2tln⁡(t))=2ln⁡(t)+3

Next, we put a=0 to find the time when the acceleration is zero: 0=2ln⁡(t)+32ln⁡(t)=−3ln⁡(t)=−32t=e−3/2

So the acceleration is zero when t=e−3/2. To find the velocity at this moment, we substitute this back into v(t) to get v(e−3/2)=2(e−3/2)ln⁡(e−3/2)+e−3/2=2e−3/2(−32)+e−3/2=−2e−3/2.

content.knowledge_point: Calculating the Velocity of a Particle at the Moment When Its Acceleration is Zero
content.problem:
A particle $P$ is traveling along the $x$-axis with displacement $s(t)$ from a fixed origin $O$ given by

$$
s(t)={t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(t),\,t\ge 0.
$$

Find the time at which the acceleration is zero, and find the value of the velocity at this moment.
content.worked_solution:
First, we calculate $v(t)$ by differentiating $s(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(t)) \\  & =2t\operatorname{ln}⁡(t)+t\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we differentiate $v(t)$ to find $a(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+2t\operatorname{ln}⁡(t)) \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡(t)+3\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we put $a=0$ to find the time when the acceleration is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡(t)+3 \\ 2\operatorname{ln}⁡(t) & =-3 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(t) & =-\frac{3}{2} \\ t & ={e}^{-3/2}\end{aligned}
$$

So the acceleration is zero when $t={e}^{-3/2}.$ To find the velocity at this moment, we substitute this back into $v(t)$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}v({e}^{-3/2}) & =2({e}^{-3/2})\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-3/2})+{e}^{-3/2} \\  & =2{e}^{-3/2}(-\frac{3}{2})+{e}^{-3/2} \\  & =-2{e}^{-3/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

a
t=1,v=−7
b
t=12,v=−83
c
t=1,v=152
d
t=32,v=−212
e
t=32,v=9
Submit

decision.explanation: Differentiating gives v(t)=6t²-18t+3 and a(t)=12t-18. Setting a(t)=0 gives t=3/2. Then v(3/2)=27/2-27+3=-21/2.

after.name: Question 14
after.problem:
A particle $P$ is traveling along the $x$-axis with displacement $s(t)$ from a fixed origin $O$ given by

$$
s(t)=2{t}^{3}-9{t}^{2}+3t-2,\,t\ge 0.
$$

Find the time at which the acceleration is zero, and find the value of the velocity at this moment.
after.worked_solution:
First, we calculate $v(t)$ by differentiating $s(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{3}-9{t}^{2}+3t-2) \\  & =6{t}^{2}-18t+3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we differentiate $v(t)$ to find $a(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6{t}^{2}-18t+3) \\  & =12t-18\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we put $a=0$ to find the time when the acceleration is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}12t-18 & =0 \\ t & =\frac{18}{12} \\ t & =\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the acceleration is zero when $t=\frac{3}{2}.$ To find the velocity at this moment, we substitute this back into $v(t)$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(\frac{3}{2}) & =6{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-18(\frac{3}{2})+3 \\  & =6(\frac{9}{4})-27+3 \\  & =\frac{27}{2}-27+3 \\  & =-\frac{21}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

A particle $P$ is traveling along the $x$-axis with displacement $s(t)$ from a fixed origin $O$ given by

$$
s(t)=2{t}^{3}-9{t}^{2}+3t-2,\,t\ge 0.
$$

Find the time at which the acceleration is zero, and find the value of the velocity at this moment.
content.worked_solution:
First, we calculate $v(t)$ by differentiating $s(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{3}-9{t}^{2}+3t-2) \\  & =6{t}^{2}-18t+3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we differentiate $v(t)$ to find $a(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6{t}^{2}-18t+3) \\  & =12t-18\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we put $a=0$ to find the time when the acceleration is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}12t-18 & =0 \\ t & =\frac{18}{12} \\ t & =\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the acceleration is zero when $t=\frac{3}{2}.$ To find the velocity at this moment, we substitute this back into $v(t)$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(\frac{3}{2}) & =6{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-18(\frac{3}{2})+3 \\  & =6(\frac{9}{4})-27+3 \\  & =\frac{27}{2}-27+3 \\  & =-\frac{21}{2}\end{aligned}
$$
